content:
A smart ring prototype developed by engineers at the University of California appears to have cracked one of the holy grails of health wearables: non-invasive blood glucose monitoring. The data is sent to a companion app on a paired iPhone.

While existing smart rings rely purely on biophysical data extracted from sensors (like those embedded in the Apple Watch), this ring works by analyzing sweat, while also tracking chemical biomarkers...

Currently, smart rings work in exactly the same way as the Apple Watch, using exactly the same sensors. These sensors can pull an impressive range of data, including resting heart rate, heart rate variability, respiratory rate, body temperature, cardio age, activity, sleep cycles and more.

But adding molecular sensors on top of the existing sensors would significantly increase the amount of health data that can be collected. According to CNET, users wouldn't even need to sweat, as the technology can draw sweat from the skin.

Engineers at the University of California, San Diego believe they have developed the world's first smart ring that uses sweat from the finger to track chemical biomarkers. The ring is currently only a prototype, but it demonstrates the potential for future smart rings to continuously monitor the body at the molecular level, rather than relying purely on biophysical data. In a paper published in Nature Communications on July 23, the engineering team reports that the new smart ring uses sweat to continuously monitor up to four of the following biochemical markers: glucose, ketones, vitamin C, uric acid, lactate, and alcohol levels.

The ring could be particularly useful for people with Type 1 diabetes.

The tests showed that its accuracy is very close to that of invasive continuous glucose monitors and blood draws.

The prototype ring is rather bulky, with a battery life of only 12 hours, but the commercial version is expected to significantly improve on both of these areas. It would be great to see what Apple's engineers could do with this technology.
